Rechecked original candidate 6ebae89f6484418b §1 and its digest. The original argument uses an inball to bound the scales. The revised hypothesis makes this argument valid, because the full-dimensional template in positive dimension contains a nonzero vector u.

For every feasible scale t, the points a(z) and a(z)+tu lie in the compact fiber, so t times the norm of u is bounded by the fiber diameter. The feasible set contains zero, and passing to the limit pointwise on J gives closedness. The maximum exists even when the fiber is lower-dimensional and only scale zero works.

Convexity of C gives the Minkowski inclusion for every two bases and interpolation parameter. Convexity of J identifies the Minkowski sum of its nonnegative multiples with the multiple by the sum, also at zero. Affineness gives the required interpolated mark, establishing concavity.
Matched the statement and Minkowski argument to original candidate 6ebae89f6484418b §1 and verified the raw source digest.

For a given z, zero is feasible because the affine mark belongs to the fiber. If t_m are feasible and tend to t, then for every u in J the points a(z)+t_m u converge inside the closed fiber to a(z)+tu. Thus feasibility is closed even in lower-dimensional fibers.

For d≥1 choose a nonzero u in J, possible by the interior assumption. Then t·|u|≤diam(C) for all feasible t, establishing the bound, attainment, and the zero-radius case. At d=0 there is no such nonzero u.

For two bases and a convex interpolation, the Minkowski combination is contained in the target fiber by convexity of C. Nonnegative multiples of the same convex J add to the multiple with the summed coefficient, using the same template point for the reverse inclusion. This works also if one or both coefficients vanish. Affineness gives the target center and the claimed concavity.
